name: QuickJS
summary: A small embeddable JavaScript engine with per-runtime heaps, per-context globals, direct stack bytecode compilation, reference-counted values, and cycle removal.

features.name: Runtime and context embedding boundary
features.description: QuickJS models a JSRuntime as an object heap and a JSContext as a Realm with its own global and system objects. Contexts may share objects within a runtime, while separate runtimes cannot exchange objects and do not support multithreading inside one runtime.
benefits: Gives embedders explicit heap and global-environment boundaries
Allows multiple contexts to share a runtime-level object space
costs: Embedder lifecycle and cross-context sharing require explicit coordination
A runtime is not a multi-threaded object-sharing boundary

features.name: Direct stack bytecode compilation
features.description: QuickJS compiles JavaScript directly to compact stack-based bytecode without an exposed parse-tree intermediate representation, computes function maximum stack size at compile time, and can serialize compiled code into generated C sources.
benefits: Keeps the interpreter and generated artifacts small
Provides a compact executable representation for embedded deployments
costs: The bytecode format is tied to a QuickJS version
A direct compiler path exposes fewer reusable intermediate boundaries

features.name: Reference counting with cycle removal
features.description: QuickJS uses reference counting for automatic and deterministic object reclamation and runs a separate cycle-removal pass when memory pressure requires it. JSValue ownership is managed through explicit duplication and freeing in the C API.
benefits: Provides a mechanism for reclaiming cyclic object structures
costs: Reference-count ownership must be respected at C API boundaries
Cycle detection adds a separate memory-management phase

features.name: Interruptible C embedding API
features.description: The C API exposes native functions, explicit exception values, memory limits, maximum stack size, and an interrupt handler called during execution so hosts can implement resource and timeout boundaries.
benefits: Lets hosts connect native operations to JavaScript values
Provides explicit controls for memory, stack, and execution interruption
costs: Native code must check and propagate JavaScript exceptions
Host callbacks remain responsible for the safety of native resources

mathematical_views.question: How do runtimes, contexts, objects, and C-owned values constrain sharing and lifetime at the embedding boundary?
assumptions: Runtimes are heap domains and contexts are global-environment domains
Object-sharing edges exist only where the API permits them
The view abstracts native allocator details and JavaScript semantic evaluation

mathematical_views.question: How do compiled stack instructions and bounded function stack sizes represent JavaScript execution?
assumptions: A bytecode frame contains an instruction position and operand stack
Compilation produces a version-specific instruction sequence
The view abstracts parser implementation, host callbacks, and processor code generation

mathematical_views.question: How do reference updates and cycle-removal transitions determine object reclamation?
assumptions: Managed objects form a graph with reference counts
Reference decrements can make acyclic objects reclaimable
A separate cycle-removal pass handles residual cyclic reachability and the view does not prove collector correctness

benefits: Explicit embeddable heap and Realm boundaries
costs: Sharing and threading restrictions require host coordination
C ownership and cycle processing add complexity
Native exception and lifetime handling remains an embedder duty
